newsitem.title: UK: City of London bets on hefty Labour majority.
newsitem.headline: City of London bets on hefty Labour majority.

text.p: Market strategists in the City of London are betting on a decisive election win for Britain's Labour party and telling clients that the outlook is set fair for the markets with Tony Blair in 10 Downing Street.
"You have to base your strategy on a Labour win with a large enough majority for them to enact their proposals," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.
He said the current consensus in London's financial markets was that Labour will be swept into power with a majority of around 100 seats.

A good guide to City thinking is provided by so-called "spread betting," a complicated and risky form of gambling enjoyed by many financial traders. Bets are taken on all sorts of events but gambling on the size of a Labour majority has reached fever pitch.
Financial bookmaker IG Index said on Monday the bets it had received point to a Labour majority of between 93 and 103 seats, while another firm, City Index, was quoting 96 to 106 seats.
Paul Barnett, political market-maker at City Index, said the spread had shot up since several Sunday newspapers splashed predictions of Labour landslides across their front pages.
"We're seeing aggressive selling of Tory seats," he said. "That spread is down out 225/231 from above 240 a week ago."
In the real world, the Conservatives went into the election campaign holding 321 seats, one less than the combined opposition total.

Stephen Yorke, head of political research at SBC Warburg, agreed with Shepperd that the election winner was not now the issue for the markets. "The size of the parliamentary majority and the following mix of fiscal and monetary policy is a far more important call."
Yorke said he would be a "seller" of the spread bets on offer, predicting a Labour majority of between 20 and 30 seats. "But that in itself would be an enormous achievement."

The worry for the markets is that just as John Major's government has been haunted by a right-wing Eurosceptic section of the Conservative Party, so a Labour government with a small majority could be at the mercy of old-style Labour left-wingers.

Major was swept back into power with a majority of 21 seats at the 1992 election but this was steadily eroded by deaths and defections, leaving him in a minority of one seat when this year's election was called.
"They obviously need a majority of more than 20," Shepperd said. "I would have thought anything more than 40 would be enough to push their programme through."

Yorke agreed that a majority of less than 20 could leave a Blair government vulnerable. "The Labour party is divided on more issues -- privatisation, tax and spending, Europe -- than the Conservatives. But there are fewer potential dissenters."

Given that a clear-cut Labour win is widely expected, Shepperd said the markets were looking well past next Thursday, to Chancellor of the Exchequer-in-waiting Gordon Brown's first meetings with Bank of England Governor Eddie George and then his budget, which will be held within two months of the election.
A monetary meeting between the Chancellor and George is pencilled in for May 7, just six days after the election.
Brown may take an early opportunity to set out his anti-inflationary credentials by raising interest rates. But few analysts expect rates to go much higher under Labour than the Conservatives.

"What we're telling clients is we expect the combination of these two events to be market-friendly," Shepperd said. "Rates won't rise as far as some fear and the fiscal stance will be as prudent as Blair has said it would be."
Labour has pledged not to increase income tax and will stick to the government's spending plans for the next two years. That is music to the markets' ears.
"You're certainly not looking at an explosion of the PSBR (budget deficit) although whether the plans are achievable on a two-to-three year view is more open to question," Shepperd said.
He said the outlook was good for UK markets to the end of the year, but maybe not beyond.
Yorke also said a Labour administration, even with a modest majority, should not do much to hurt the markets this year.

"The period between May 2 and the end of July is going to be important, not just for this year but the whole parliament. But Blair's standing in his party will be so strong for the first year of government, he will get through what he wants to."
